passages.original: " Nunc Campaniam petamus." Iam delicata fastidio sunt : " Inculta videantur, Bruttios et Lucaniae saltus persequamur." Aliquid tamen inter deserta amoeni requiritur, in quo luxuriosi oculi longo locorum horrentium squalore releventur: " Tarentum petatur laudatusque portus et hiberna caeli mitioris et regio vel antiquae satis opulenta turbae." Nimis diu a plausu et fragore aures vacaverunt, iuvat iam et humano sanguine frui : " Iam flectamus cursum ad urbem." Aliud ex alio iter suscipitur et spectacula spectaculis mutantur. Ut ait Lucretius :
passages.english: "Now let us make for Campania." Soon refinement is distasteful: "Let us see uncultivated places, let us go after the Bruttii and the forest-pastures of Lucania." Yet among the wilds something pleasant is wanted, in which eyes used to luxury may be relieved from the long squalor of rugged places: "Let Tarentum be our goal, and its praised harbour, and the winter quarters of a milder sky, and a region rich enough even for the crowds of old." Too long have the ears been free of applause and din; now it pleases [us] to enjoy human blood as well: "Now let us turn our course to the city." One journey is undertaken after another, and spectacles are exchanged for spectacles. As Lucretius says:
passages.notes: The passage ends with the introduction of a quotation from Lucretius that is not included. "Even for the crowds of old" (vel antiquae satis opulenta turbae) refers to the large population Tarentum once supported; the phrasing is compressed. "Human blood" refers to gladiatorial shows in Rome.

passages.original: Vix tibi esset facultas dilectus felicioris, si inter Platonas et Xenophontas et illum Socratici fetus proventum bonos quaereres, aut si tibi potestas Catonianae fieret aetatis, quae plerosque dignos tulit, qui Catonis saeculo nascerentur, sicut multos peiores quam umquam alias maximorumque molitores scelerum ; utraque enim turba opus erat, ut Cato posset intellegi : habere debuit et bonos, quibus se adprobaret, et malos, in quibus vim suam experiretur.
passages.english: You would scarcely have the opportunity of a happier choice if you were looking for good men among men like Plato and Xenophon and that whole crop of Socrates' offspring, or if you were given access to the age of Cato. That age produced a great many men worthy to be born in Cato's time, just as it produced many who were worse than at any other time, contrivers of the greatest crimes. Both crowds were needed so that Cato could be understood: he had to have good men, whose approval he could win, and bad men, against whom he could test his strength.
passages.notes: "Platonas et Xenophontas" (plural) means "men like Plato and Xenophon."

passages.original: Reverti unde veneris quid grave est ? Male vivet quisquis nesciet bene mori. Huic itaque primum rei pretium detrahendum est et spiritus inter vilia numerandus. Gladiatores, ut ait Cicero, invisos habemus, si omni modo vitam impetrare cupiunt; favemus, si contemptum eius prae se ferunt. Idem evenire nobis scias ; saepe enim causa moriendi est timide mori.
passages.english: What is hard about returning to where you came from? Whoever does not know how to die well will live badly. So the first thing is to strip this of its value and to count the breath of life among cheap things. Gladiators, as Cicero says, we hate if they are eager to obtain their life by any means; we favour them if they openly display contempt for it. Know that the same happens to us; for often the cause of dying is dying fearfully.
